newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil court to rule on key telecom bill Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Brazil court to rule on key telecom bill Thursday.

text.p: Brazil's Supreme Federal Tribunal (STF), the country's highest court, is scheduled to rule Thursday on whether a 1996 law laying out the framework for the deregulation of the telecommunications sector is constitutional or not.

The STF decision is important as a ruling declaring the law unconstitutional would delay for several months government plans to open up the multi-billion dollar telecom sector until a new general telecom bill is approved by Congress.

The same ruling could also suspend the tender for Band B concessions which is scheduled to take place on April 7 and which has lined up some of the biggest names in the international telecommunications industry.

The suit against the government was brought by left-wing opposition parties who claim a so-called 1996 Minimum Telecommunications Law breaches the constitution by altering the terms in which the Band A cellular phone concessions were granted. The Band A system is currently being exploited by state regional telephone operators which function under Telebras, Brazil's federal telecom holding.

The Brazilian government would like to separate the profitable Band A concessions from the regional operators and sell them to private investors before the privatization of wire phone services which are not expected to take place until mid 1998.
The opposition parties also question the role of a powerful new telecommunications regulating agency the creation of which is included in the Minimum Telecommunications Law.
The new agency would be responsible for granting telecom concessions, setting policy and remain largely independent of government and congressional interference.

Market analysts say the suit against the government is a last ditch attempt by the opposition to slow down the privatization program and win leverage in the on-going debate over the general telecommunications law. They said they doubted the STF would declare the Minimum Telecommunications Law unconstitutional. "The government thinks it has a strong case and that the court will rule in its favor," said a telecoms analyst at a local investment bank who asked not to be identified.

PT legislators say their aim is to build a more solid legal framework for Brazil's future telecom sector. They say they are not opposed to privatization or competition in the industry, but claim the government is trying to force through legislation which will favor only a handful of friendly investors.

While the plan of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's administration is to see Telebras dismembered and extinguished, opposition legislators believe the state telecom holding should be preserved and strengthened to compete in the new deregulated business environment.
"We want to discuss this ridiculous idea of dividing up Telebras. It is contrary to what serious countries are doing all over the world," said Worker's Party congressman Walter Pinheiro.
